prompt.context: Your client is Walter Black Industries, a privately owned chemical manufacturing company based in Albuquerque, New Mexico that specializes in producing car wash chemicals. The client has two major products, Car Wash A and Truck Wash A. After a series of aggressive acquisitions 5 years ago, the client has become a market leader, but revenue growth has become stagnant in the last 2 years.
prompt.question: The client would like us to identify opportunities to increase revenue by 30% without reducing profit margins. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's current revenue and profit margin?
clarifying_info.a: The client made $1B last year (60% from Car Wash A, 40% from Truck Wash A) with a profit margin of 40%. The client would like to keep overall profit margins across all products at or above 40%.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client handle distribution and packaging?
clarifying_info.a: No. The client only sells chemicals. The customer pays for all distribution and packaging costs.

clarifying_info.q: What is the industry growth rate?
clarifying_info.a: The car and truck wash chemicals industry has been growing by 2% on average over the last 10 years. It is difficult for both the customer and end customer of the product to differentiate between product quality.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have new products in development?
clarifying_info.a: The client currently has no new products in the pipeline. Formulations for new products take 5 years to develop and have a high chance of failure (85%).
The client only sells to chemical wholesale distributors — the top 5 wholesale distributors who control 95% of the global market share.

There are three main competitors. Along with the client, these four companies control 90% of the entire market. Capital costs are high and there are no concerns over new market entrants. No potential acquisition targets are available.

exhibits.title: Competitive Benchmarking
exhibits.shows: Two side-by-side bar charts comparing Revenue ($M) split into Cost and Profit for Walter Black Industries, Competitor A, Competitor B, and Competitor C — one chart for Car Wash Chemicals and one for Truck Wash Chemicals.

data.bars_shown: Walter Black Industries, Competitor A, Competitor B, Competitor C; each bar divided into Cost (lower segment) and Profit (upper segment)

exhibits.title: Pricing Analysis
exhibits.shows: A table listing current pricing, cost per tote, average annual totes sold, and average annual revenue for Car Wash A and Truck Wash A.

framework: Revenue growth levers: Price vs. Volume
Price: current pricing vs. competitors, elasticity of demand, potential to raise or lower prices
Volume — existing customers: increase share of wallet, increase purchase frequency
Volume — new customers: expand customer base within existing channels (5 distributors), enter new geographies
Volume — new channels: sell directly or through new distributors
New products/services: adjacent chemical products (ruled out — 5-yr dev time, 85% failure rate)
Acquisitions: inorganic growth (ruled out — no targets available)
Margin check: any revenue strategy must preserve ≥40% overall profit margin

questions.prompt: What insights can you derive from Exhibit 1 (Competitive Benchmarking)?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates identify: (1) Client has ~20% dollar market share in car wash category and significantly higher margins than competitors; the competitor with the highest total revenue has the lowest margins. (2) Client has ~20% dollar market share in truck wash category but significantly lower margins than competitors. (3) The car wash market is roughly 50% larger than the truck wash market. Candidate should recognize that cost reduction is a distractor — costs are similar across competitors — and focus on the margin gap in truck wash as a pricing opportunity.

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit 2 and the following elasticity data, identify the optimal pricing strategy: Car Wash A — a $1 change in price/gal changes demand by 50,000 totes; Truck Wash A — a $1 change in price/gal changes demand by 100,000 totes. The client can only change prices in $1 increments. Each tote is 200 gallons.
questions.guidance: Candidate should determine revenue-maximizing price for each product. Two valid approaches: (1) Table approach — build a price/quantity/revenue table and find the peak. (2) Formula/calculus approach — derive quantity as a function of price, then maximize revenue = price × quantity. Optimal conclusion: decrease Car Wash A to $8/gal and increase Truck Wash A to $6/gal, yielding total revenue of $1,360M (+36%). A simpler acceptable answer is to raise Truck Wash A to $5, $6, or $7 (all exceed the 30% revenue target while maintaining margins).

math.setup: Each tote = 200 gal. Revenue per tote = $/gal × 200. Revenue = ($/gal × 200) × totes sold. Elasticity: Car Wash A Q = 800K − 50K×P (anchor: at $10, Q=300K → 800K−50K×10=300K ✓). Truck Wash A Q = 1200K − 100K×P (anchor: at $2, Q=1000K → 1200K−100K×2=1000K ✓).
steps: Profit check — Car Wash A: revenue/tote = $8×200=$1,600; cost/tote=$1,000; profit/tote=$600; totes=400K; profit=$240M. Truck Wash A: revenue/tote=$6×200=$1,200; cost/tote=$300; profit/tote=$900; totes=600K; profit=$540M. Total profit=$780M. Margin=$780M/$1,360M≈57% > 40% ✓.
math.answer: Optimal strategy: lower Car Wash A to $8/gal and raise Truck Wash A to $6/gal. New total revenue = $1,360M (+36%); overall profit margin ≈57%. Both goals are met.

recommendation: Recommend a two-part pricing change: reduce Car Wash A from $10 to $8/gal and increase Truck Wash A from $2 to $6/gal.
This increases total revenue from $1B to $1.36B (+36%), exceeding the 30% growth target, while raising the profit margin from 40% to approximately 57%.
risks: Competitor retaliation / price war, particularly in the truck wash segment where the price increase is significant
Lowering Car Wash A price may negatively affect brand perception or signal lower quality to customers
Large price increase in Truck Wash A ($2→$6) may cause distributors to seek alternative suppliers or negotiate volume discounts
Assumes linear demand elasticity holds across the full price range; actual demand response may differ
next_steps: Coordinate with the sales team to communicate and implement new pricing with the top 5 wholesale distributors
Perform customer segmentation analysis to determine whether differentiated pricing for individual customers could further improve revenue
Monitor volume and margin by product closely in the first 2–3 months after implementation to validate elasticity assumptions
Explore whether any complementary services (e.g., technical support, formulation consulting) could add revenue without product development lead time
